sweep_summary: Nubi (nubi1253) is in the catalog as lexical on Luffin's APiCS survey 63 with Gussenhoven's 4-page TAL-2006 proceedings paper as secondary. this search of works with stress in the title had one title hit, Gussenhoven 2006 'Between stress and tone in Nubi word prosody' (Phonology 23: 193-223), already in the per-language bibliography; the Radboud OA publisher's version was already saved held by the project (downloaded 2026-09-16 via an Internet Archive copy; the repository host itself not reachable by automated download by automated download) and I read it in full. It is the authoritative first-hand study: obligatory, culminative, metrically bound accent within a right-edge three-syllable window, penultimate by default (syllabic trochee) with lexically specified antepenultimate and final accent that are 'common', H tone on every accented syllable, no quantity contrasts, morphological accent in nouns (plural = final) and verbs (stem/gerund/passive differ by accent alone), plus phrasal Gerund Deaccenting and Accent Shift. It refines rather than changes the classification: lexical stands (position not computable from phonological shape), with a penultimate default and H-tone realisation worth recording; it should replace the TAL abstract as the deciding source alongside Luffin. I also read Wellens' 2003 Nijmegen dissertation (held by the project, pp.42-43), which confirms the three-syllable window, source-language retention of stress, the sába/sabá minimal pairs and the plural/gerund/passive shifts (but adds a lexical-tone analysis Gussenhoven rejects); it is not in the catalog bibliography and could be added. written at Nothing remains unread; no acquisitions needed.

new_statements.reading: One obligatory, culminative word accent per lexical word, realised as an H tone, confined to the last three syllables. Penultimate is the default (right-edge syllabic trochee) for non-verb polysyllables; antepenultimate and final accent are 'common' and must be lexically pre-specified (feet in the lexicon), so surface position is not predictable from syllable count or weight (there are no quantity contrasts, p.196). Morphology moves the accent (plural = final; verb stem = mostly antepenult, gerund = penult, passive = final accented vowel), and phrasal deaccenting/accent shift apply postlexically. This is the full, instrumentally supported version of the 4-page TAL-2006 proceedings paper the catalog cites as secondary; it keeps the catalog's lexical coding but makes explicit that it is a penultimate-default system with lexically marked exceptions inside a three-syllable window and with fixed H-tone realisation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One word stress per lexical word, restricted to a three-syllable right-edge window (final, penult or antepenult); its position is lexically fixed as a reflex of the stress of the source form (Arabic, Swahili, Luganda, English), so it is not predictable from syllable count or weight (no quantity contrasts; stressed vowels are lengthened, and stress is also carried by loudness and high pitch). Function words are unstressed. Some lexical minimal pairs ('saba 'seven' vs sa'ba 'tomorrow'; 'zina 'adornment' vs zi'na 'adultery'; 'kede EMPH vs ke'de SUBJ) and free variants ('masgit ~ mas'giti, 'madrasa ~ mad'rasa) exist. Morphology moves stress: plural -a takes final stress ('bagara ~ baga'ra), predicative vs attributive demonstrative ('wede vs we'de), bare verb usually initial (= antepenult in trisyllables, 'kasulu), gerund penult, passive final; tone plays a limited independent role (infinitive H on all syllables, H on passive/infinitive of monosyllabic verbs).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress of source language usually retained; only exceptionally shifted in borrowings (English 'cholera > ko'lera); free variation in a few words ('masgit ~ mas'giti, 'fitna ~ fi'tina, 'dirisa ~ di'risa); bare verbs of types (d) ni'situ, (e) we'di, (f) fata'ran keep non-initial stress; 'ita 'saba ke'fin? has initial stress on 'saba unlike sa'ba 'morning' (fn.48); fn.46 reports Heine (1982: 27) treating Kenyan Nubi as tonal with stress predictable on the first high tone of the word.
new_statements.identity_note: Wellens 2003 describes Ugandan Nubi (Bombo, Arua, Gulu speakers; she abbreviates UN) and contrasts it with Kenyan Nubi (KN, Heine 1982) and Juba Arabic; Gussenhoven 2006 in the existing statement is also based on Ugandan (Bombo) speakers. Heine's tonal analysis, cited second-hand by Wellens, is of Kenyan Nubi.

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict. Wellens 2003 (Ugandan Nubi) and the existing Gussenhoven 2006 statement agree that one word stress/accent falls on one of the last three syllables, is lexically fixed, and is moved by morphology (plural and passive final, gerund penult, bare verb initial/antepenult). The only differences are of characterisation, not placement: Wellens calls it stress (length + loudness + high pitch) with a marginal independent tone in verb inflection and does not name a penultimate default (she attributes penult to Swahili loans and derives all positions from source-form stress), whereas Gussenhoven treats it as an H-tone accent with penultimate as the default foot. Wellens also reports (fn.46, p.222) that Heine 1982 analyses Kenyan Nubi as tonal with stress predictable on the first high tone of the word; that concerns the Kenyan variety and was not opened here. The Owens 1977/1978 thesis could not be obtained, so it neither confirms nor contradicts.

sources.quote: Stress is confined to one of the last three syllables in the word. ... Vowels in stressed syllables are mainly articulated long, whereas vowels in unstressed syllables are generally short. Stress is also marked by loudness and by high pitch. Word stress in Nubi much depends on the stress patterns in the source languages of the Nubi words. ... Although the words may have been subjected to phonemic changes, stress is usually retained. ... In a few cases, stress is lexically distinctive ... 'saba 'seven' - sa'ba 'tomorrow' ... In plural formation as well, stress is shifted to the final syllable [pp.42-43]
sources.locator: §2.1.4 'Stress, pitch, and tone', pp.42-43 (dissertation pagination); table 8 p.43; §2.2.4 p.68 (summary of stress variation)
sources.note: Stress in one of the last three syllables; correlates: vowel length, loudness, high pitch; position largely inherited from source-language stress (Arabic, Swahili penult, Luganda); a few lexically distinctive pairs ('saba 'seven' vs sa'ba 'tomorrow', 'zina vs zi'na); grammatical stress shift to final syllable in plurals and passives, to penult in gerunds; free variants for some words ('masgit ~ mas'giti). Wellens additionally posits lexical tone independent of stress (table 8), which Gussenhoven 2006 rejects. This is the source of Luffin's sába/sabá example.
